Chapter 23 — First Reading: Recipes and Seed Stock
Chapter 41 — The Vestibule at First Light

spans.text: The Foundation kept its board room above a flower shop on Pinellas Avenue, two flights up a narrow stair, and Nicolette took the stair the way she took every stair in the Greektown blocks, slow at the bend and steady on the landing. The carpet was the color of mastic resin before bleeding, a pale clouded yellow chosen years ago by someone for the room it was meant to introduce. The room had not been changed since.

She was three minutes early. She had walked the four blocks from the Historical Society under a sky the off-white of October on the Gulf, setting the questions she expected in their order of likelihood and putting aside the two answers she was not going to give. She would offer the third.
Margaret Halikias-Demos sat at the head of the long table with two folders squared in front of her and the morning light cutting through the slatted blinds onto the back of her hand.
Kyria Pappas. Sit anywhere.
Nicolette took the chair to Margaret's left, the one the Foundation kept for its archivist of record, which she had been for three years running.
The board met last evening. The pledge is confirmed.

Margaret slid one folder across the table, manila, the Foundation's small embossed seal at the upper left. Nicolette did not open it. She had drafted the budget memo Margaret was confirming, two months ago, and she knew the figure on the second page.
Seventy thousand,
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: Margaret said.
Which is what you asked for. The board was generous and the board was also unanimous, so I want a moment before we go to the next item.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: She folded her small freckled hands over the closed folder. She was sixty-one and had been board president eight years. Her grandfather had owned three boats out of the Sponge Exchange in the 1920s; her father had married into the diocese; her mother had taught fourth grade at the parish school. Margaret had spent her adult life inheriting in stages.
I want to be plain about why the board moved,
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: she said.

We have had three exhibition proposals from the Historical Society in five years and we have funded one. This one we can carry. There are sponge exhibitions. There are parish exhibitions. There is no exhibition that holds the mastic and the sponge as one import economy, the same boats, the same families, the same parish ledgers. That is your proposal. The board saw it. The board pledged.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: She paused.
I want a centerpiece.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: Nicolette had expected the sentence at this seam in the conversation and had decided not to step in front of it. She let it sit the length of a slow breath.
What kind of centerpiece.
spans.speaker: Nicolette

spans.text: A serious one. A manuscript. A ledger. Something a visitor can stand in front of and feel the years are present in the room. We have the receipts. The receipts are good. The receipts are not a centerpiece.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: They can be.
spans.speaker: Nicolette

spans.text: Kyria Pappas.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: Margaret smiled, and the smile was not insincere; it belonged to a woman who had used the word kyria for forty years as a small precision.
You are the archivist. I am the donor. Tell me I am wrong about what a centerpiece is and I will listen.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: There was a long version of the argument and a short one. Nicolette had given the long version once at a regional archivists' meeting in Atlanta, had been right, and had changed no minds. The short version was that the centerpiece for an exhibition on a trade was the trade's own paper, because the paper was where the trade had happened. It had not held in Atlanta either. She kept it.
I take your point,
spans.speaker: Nicolette

spans.text: she said.
Good. Now I am going to ask you a question, because the board asked me to. Would the Chios manuscript be available.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: Nicolette did not move her hands.
Which Chios manuscript.
spans.speaker: Nicolette

spans.text: The codex. The Mastic Codex. The cooperative one. The one the monastery keeps.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: I know which manuscript you mean. I do not know whether it would be available.
spans.speaker: Nicolette

spans.text: I would like you to find out,
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: Margaret said.

The board has framed the pledge as conditional on the centerpiece. I am telling you that in the spirit it was framed in, which is vision and not leverage. The board's vision is the centerpiece. The board's instrument is the pledge. Hear that as one sentence said twice, not as two sentences.
spans.speaker: Margaret

spans.text: The cadence was rehearsed, and the rehearsal was a courtesy rather than a concealment. Margaret had offered leverage as its own antonym before anyone had reached for the word, which told Nicolette that someone in the room last evening had used it and Margaret had argued the room out of it. She would not have to learn who.
I hear it,
she said.

I will be plain in return. I do not know the codex's condition. I do not know the monastery's loan policy, or that there is one. The monastery has held the codex a century, by what I have read. It has not traveled.
It has not. We checked.
And if it cannot.
Then we will talk. The board has not asked you to deliver the codex. The board has asked you to learn whether it can be the centerpiece of an exhibition the board is ready to fund.
Margaret lifted her coffee cup and set it down again without drinking.

There is a person I want to mention before you go. The Foundation is asking through its own contacts after a private collector with useful contacts in Eastern Mediterranean archival circles. Such a man can be helpful on access. He would not be a Foundation employee and he would not be on the board. If the monastery returns a polite no, it may help to have a second channel. I am not asking you to use it. I am telling you it is there.
You are not naming him.

I have no name yet. And I want you to understand the second channel is the Foundation's and not yours. The Foundation will find the collector. The Foundation keeps the relationship. If the introduction is offered, it comes through me.
The smile came back, smaller.
I do not like Foundation business that pretends it is not Foundation business.
Neither do I.
That is one of the reasons we wanted you for this.

Nicolette set the compliment down on the table beside the folder. Margaret took her through the disbursement schedule, three tranches, one at signing, one at sixty days, one at opening night, confirmed the donor acknowledgment on the wall plate and the timeline of twelve weeks from the director's sign-off, and stood. The meeting had run thirty-eight minutes.
Nicolette went down the narrow stair to Pinellas Avenue, where the delivery man was loading a hand truck with white roses for a wedding she would not attend, and walked the four blocks back.

These were the blocks her grandmother had walked with a string bag and a coupon book in the 1950s. At the foot of Dodecanese Boulevard the Sponge Exchange held its mid-morning trade, the tourists inside it and the boat captains around it. She looked at it for one second and walked on.

The reading room ran the length of the east side of the Old Exchange Building, on the second floor of what had been the original Sponge Exchange counting house, put up in 1908. Three tall windows gave onto the market across the parking lot, the masts of the sponge boats visible above the roof of the seafood restaurant between. The room was empty, as it usually was on a Wednesday in October, but for the volunteer at the front desk, who waved over the day's newspaper.

The Halikias-Demos donation sat on the survey table at the back of the room: twelve cardboard archive boxes, each labeled in Margaret's careful donor hand, HALIKIAS / DEMOS COLLECTION, MASTIC-AND-SPONGE IMPORT PAPERS, 1908 TO 1947, BOX X OF XII. Margaret's father had handed them to the previous director eleven years ago, in the early stages of the illness that took him the following year. The previous director had accessioned the donation at the collection level and retired before he catalogued it item by item. Nicolette had begun the cataloguing in September. She had finished three boxes. Nine to go, twelve weeks to go, a centerpiece to ask about, in that order.
She stood with her coat still on and her hand on the lid of box four and thought about where to begin.

She thought first of Brother Makarios, whom she did not know, whose codex she had read of twice in her life: once in a 1972 article in a Greek folklore journal her grandmother had saved, which called it a monastic registry of mastic-village agricultural production from 1908 forward and said nothing about loan or access; once in a dissertation footnote that cited the article and added nothing.

She thought second of the cooperative, whose archive was at Pyrgi on Chios and whose branch office at Pothia, across on Kalymnos, kept the Chian copies of the harvest registries for the years her boxes covered. If the monastery held the codex and the cooperative held the registries, the two custodies had a relationship, and the office would know whether the codex traveled, and to what kind of host. She would write them a careful letter. The Foundation would go unmentioned in it.

She thought third of Margaret's collector, who did not yet have a name even in her own thoughts. She held him only as the second channel, a thing that existed and not yet a thing she would be asked to use.
She hung her coat on the hook, moved box four to the cataloguing table, and wrote across the top of a fresh log page: BOX 4, RESUMED, item 47. Then she lifted the next folder and began.

She catalogued the way she always did, the headings written out longhand before she entered them, the provenance chain in the right margin of the log in the small precise hand her grandmother had taught her at seven for the marking of school papers.

The right archive was always the public archive. It was the discipline she had practiced for fifteen years. If the codex could be borrowed it would be borrowed under public-loan terms; if it could not, the exhibition would hold its center in the receipts, the way she had thought from the start it could.

She was thirty-eight years old, the staff archivist at the Tarpon Springs Historical Society, with a pledge in a folder on the corner of the table, nine boxes of trade paper, twelve weeks, and a letter to draft to a Pothia cooperative office she had never written to.
She catalogued item 47, item 48, item 49.

She lifted the receipt for item 50 and laid the ruled magnifying lens beside it, the way she did for any receipt with handwritten field marks. The date in the upper-right corner read like every date in box four, an ordinary shipping date in the bookkeeper's pencil. Then something in the pencil stroke of the month caught at her, a half-degree off the others, the way a single thread sits proud of the weave. The afternoon was nearly gone and the entry could wait. She set the receipt a half-sheet's width to the right, in the small offset she kept for a thing she meant to come back to, and laid the lens across it to hold the place. She would read it Friday.
She did not yet know what she had set aside.

On Friday the reading room was empty, the volunteer not yet in, the ceiling vent giving her nothing but the building's own settling. Nicolette gave the first hour to the catalogue terminal, clearing the queue from Thursday, and then drew item 50 back from the offset where she had left it Wednesday under the lens.

It was a cooperative-printed receipt for a Chios mastic shipment. A single sheet, eight and a half by four and a half inches, the cooperative seal at the upper left, the printed columns faded from blue toward gray. The bookkeeper had filled it in with a pencil worn round, so the strokes carried a slight smudge of graphite. It was the same hand that had filled out items forty-seven through forty-nine. She had catalogued that hand twelve times in three weeks and could read it now the way she read her own.

Top line, in Greek: shipment, mastic resin, Chios. Quantity in the right-margin column in a second hand, the office manager's, in fountain pen, the okka measure converted to kilograms. Buyer on the third line, the Tarpon trading partnership the Halikias-Demos fleet had run its mastic side through in the twenties, dissolved in 1931. Date in the upper-right corner: 14 February 1923.
She wrote out the heading, the accession-fragment line, the right-margin notation, the way she did for any Chios receipt from the twenties. Then she looked at the date again.

The mastic harvest on Chios was a summer harvest. She knew it the way she knew the streets of Greektown, from before she could remember learning it. Her grandmother had bled the trees as a girl in a mastic village south of the Chian town, before the family came across to Tarpon, and had described the incising every August of Nicolette's childhood: the small clean cuts in the bark with the kentos, the swept ground beneath the trees, the white tears forming in the heat.

The tree was bled in stages from the middle of July to the middle of September. The tears were lifted a week or two after each incision, sorted and cleaned in the village courtyards, and the season's resin left the Chian ports in October and November, by way of the broker at Piraeus, before the winter storms closed the crossings. That was the partnership's window. A February shipment had no crop behind it and no weather for it. February was not ordinary.
So the month was the snag. She set the lens on the receipt.

Under the glass the date was not 14 February. The mark she had read as a one was the bookkeeper's leading flourish, the small ascending stroke he made to open the day-of-month field. The numeral under it was a four, looped at the top the way he looped every four in the box. 4 February 1923. Still February. She corrected the entry and set the receipt in the catalogued pile.
The lens had told her she could not always trust the first reading. She kept it out.

Item 51 was a parish-attested invoice, June 1923, a clean provenance chain. Item 52 was a cooperative-printed receipt for Chios mastic, the same bookkeeper, the partnership as buyer. Date: 22 March 1924. Months past the window's close, with no crop on the trees. She catalogued the receipt, and then set it half a sheet's width to the right, in the offset.
Item 53, a parish invoice. No offset.

Item 54, a cooperative receipt. Date: 28 April 1925. A late shipment could run past the window for cause she had catalogued before: weather at Piraeus, a delayed grading, a broker's schedule, an insurance arbitration over a contested grade. The late ones she had catalogued in the cooperative records at the graduate library moved by the end of December. Twenty-eight April was months past that. Offset.

Item 55: 11 March 1926. Offset. Item 56: 6 February 1927. She catalogued it slowly, the quantity consistent with a partnership winter allocation, and then set it in the offset too. She pulled item 50 back out of the catalogued pile and laid it with the others. Five.
She wrote the five dates in a column at the foot of the log page.
4 February 1923. 22 March 1924. 28 April 1925. 11 March 1926. 6 February 1927.

All five fell outside the partnership's shipping window, in the months when no resin crossed. She marked each date with a small f in the right margin, for further. She had set them apart from the box before she had decided to, and the setting apart was itself the reason.
She did not write the word cluster in the log. The column was the cluster.

She catalogued forward without stopping on it. Item 58, a cooperative receipt dated 19 February 1928: she added the date to the column and left the receipt in its place, because the column had taken over the offset's job. Six. Item 59, 3 March 1929. Seven. Item 60, 25 April 1930. Eight.

By the time she set the lid on box four and rolled the dolly to the survey table, she had catalogued through item seventy-nine, the last in the box, and the column held twenty-three dates across the twenty-five Chios mastic receipts box four contained. The other two, items seventy-one and seventy-four, were dated October 1932. October was the autumn shipping window, the window the partnership had used most heavily through the twenties. Same bookkeeper, same office manager, same buyer. The only thing that set them apart from the twenty-three was that they landed where a shipment should land.

Twenty-three dates in February, March, or April, across the years from 1923 through 1932, in one bookkeeper's hand, for one buyer. She caught herself starting to phrase what they were and put the phrasing down. They were not yet anything past that.
She wrote at the foot of the column: receipts tagged f for further. Frequency check pending, boxes five through twelve. She underlined the word frequency once.
The director came down from the third floor at a quarter past noon and stopped in the doorway.

Margaret sent the pledge confirmation. The board has signed. I have you down for the exhibition planning meeting Tuesday at nine, Margaret on the call. I would like a draft of the exhibition memo by Monday end of day, so the three of us walk into Tuesday with the same sentence in our mouths. Where are you in the cataloguing.
Box four is done. Eight to go.
At your pace, that holds the timeline.
It holds the timeline.

He was sixty-four, careful, two years from a retirement he was not ready to take, and he had a habit of standing an extra moment in a doorway when he had been given the answer he wanted, as if leaving too quickly would unsettle it. He read finding aids and he read the budget. He did not catalogue. He did not ask whether the cataloguing had turned up anything.
Tuesday at nine,
he said, and went upstairs.

She had not lied to him. Every answer had been exact. She had not said that twenty-three receipts in box four carried dates that sat where mastic did not ship, because twenty-three receipts without an explanation were a cataloguer's note, not a director's note, and very far from a donor's. She wrote in the right margin: do not raise Tuesday. Writing it made the holding deliberate in a way the silence in the doorway had not, and she let herself feel the difference before she set it down.

At one she moved box five to the table and went through it at the pace of a content survey, lifting only the cooperative-printed receipts for Chios shipments to the partnership. Box five covered 1933 to 1937. Nineteen such receipts. Seventeen fell in February, March, or April. Two fell in October.

The seventeen did not scatter across the early-year span. They settled into three narrow bands she could already draw without the log in front of her, one in the second week of February, one across the back of March, one in the last days of April, the same three places the twenty-three from box four had landed. Errors scattered. Transcription slips scattered. A bookkeeper miscopying a four as a one made a single wrong stroke in a single field; it did not arrange itself into three bands across fifteen years of one man's careful hand. She did not write that down either. She would not put a conclusion on the page before the page had earned it.

Turning the third of the seventeen under the lamp, she saw something she had passed over in box four. Three faint pencil marks in the right margin, close together, low on the sheet, the kind of marks she had read on the first pass as smudges from a thumb or a sorting tray. She turned the other box-five receipts to the margin. The marks were on all seventeen, in the same place, set down hard enough that the pressure had scored the paper. She could feel them under her fingertip on the back of the sheet.
She added the seventeen dates to the column. It ran to forty. She wrote: boxes six through twelve to survey Monday; check right margins for pencil marks. She closed the log.

Then she drafted the letter to the Pothia cooperative office in her field notebook. Three paragraphs in careful Greek, the cooperative-bookkeeper precision her grandmother had given her braided into the precision the job had given her. She introduced herself, the Society, the Halikias-Demos donation. She asked for the office's published-record account of the Chios mastic shipping convention across 1923 to 1947, and for guidance on a frequency question she would phrase more precisely in a follow-up. The Foundation went unmentioned. So did the exhibition. So did the codex. She copied it clean onto Society stationery and put it in her bag.

Athens Street held the afternoon. At the foot of Dodecanese Boulevard the Sponge Exchange held its afternoon trade, and she looked at it for one second and walked on. She mailed the letter and walked home with 22 March 1924 still in her head, a shipping date for a partnership dissolved before she was born, doing whatever it was doing that she had not yet given a name to.
